Chapter 1
Talking to a Model
This chapter builds one operation in TypeScript, field by field: you send
some text to a server, and text comes back. An agentic workflow rests
on that operation. Every diagram, review, judge and guard rule in the
twelve chapters after this one is that single operation wrapped in struc-
ture.
What the thing on the other end actually is
A large language model — LLM for short — is a very large mathe-
matical function that takes a sequence of text and produces a probability
distribution over what text comes next. It was fitted to that job by be-
ing shown an enormous quantity of text and repeatedly adjusted until
its guesses about what followed got good. The result is a fixed set of
numbers, called weights, that do not change while you use them.

That
point is the training cutoff , and after it the model knows nothing — not
because it refuses to answer, but because it has no way to distinguish
“after my cutoff” from “does not exist.” Ask about a library released
last month and you will not get “I don’t know.” You will get a fluent,
well-structured answer about a plausible library with plausible functions.
This applies to calling an API that changes. A model fitted before a
parameter was removed will keep using it, and a model fitted before a
new one existed will not reach for it. Both failures look identical from
your side — code that reads perfectly and returns a 400 .
Warning: A model is most confidently wrong about the API of
a fast-moving library, and next most about the library’s own best
practices. From inside the weights, the version it learned is the
library.

Introduction
Figure 1: A task comes in at the top. Your program builds a request and calls
the model, which picks what happens next but cannot run anything itself — it
can only name a tool and wait. Your program is what runs it, and the result
goes into the next request, so each pass through the loop carries everything
the earlier passes produced. The tools are where things actually change: a file,
a row in a database, a call to a service somewhere else. When the model
names no tool the loop ends, and the answer that leaves at the bottom is a
report on work that has already happened.
1

Giving the Model Hands 41
Watch what happens when you ask for something that needs two steps.
Change the request to:
Read demo/src/slugify.ts and demo/src/cli.ts, then tell me whether the CLI
would print an empty line for the input "///".
The model asks to read one file and you send it. It then asks for the
second file, and tool.ts , whose second loop prints only text blocks,
prints nothing, or a sentence of narration, and exits. The program does
nothing with a second tool_use , because it was written with the number
two hard-coded into it.
The fix is not more code but less structure: stop writing “first request,
second request” and write “keep going until it says it is done.”
That is a loop, and it is the entire subject of the next chapter, which is
also where the thing you have been building finally gets its name.

Now go through the request slowly, because five of those lines are con-
cepts every later chapter uses.
The request, field by field
messages and the shape of a conversation
The messages array is the entire input to the model, and it is a list of
message objects. A message is one contribution to the exchange, and it
has exactly two parts that matter here: a role , saying who is speaking,
and content, saying what they said.
There are two roles you will write by hand:
• user — you, or your program acting on your behalf.
• assistant — the model.

Talking to a Model 15
The array must begin with a user message, and conventionally the two
alternate. The complete array — every message in it, in order — is
what we will call the conversation , and when we are talking about it
as something to inspect rather than something to send, the transcript .
The array is the input : it is neither a reference to a session on An-
thropic’s servers nor a pointer to a conversation ID, but the literal text
of everything that has been said so far, sent again, in full, on every single
request.
model
The model field carries the model ID from setup.ts , and it has no
default: every request must say which model it wants. Different models
are different functions with different weights, and the same request to
two of them can produce different answers.
max_tokens
max_tokens is a hard ceiling on how much the model is allowed to pro-
duce in this response.

202 Appendix A: Glossary
context editing — Chapter 4, 04-what-it-forgets.md . An API fea-
ture that deletes old tool results from a conversation rather than sum-
marising them. Compaction is lossy about everything; context editing
is lossless about what it keeps.
context rot — Chapter 4, 04-what-it-forgets.md . The degradation
in a model’s attention to any particular piece of its input as that input
grows. It produces no error and no warning, only answers that are worse.
context window — Chapter 1, 01-talking-to-a-model.md . The max-
imum number of tokens allowed in a single request and its response com-
bined. A hard limit: exceed it and the API returns an error rather than
dropping the oldest part.
conversation — Chapter 1, 01-talking-to-a-model.md . The com-
plete messages array, in order.

64 What It Knows and Forgets
Prompt caching stores the beginning of your request on Anthropic’s
servers so that identical beginnings on later requests do not have to be
processed again. Cached input is billed at a small fraction of the normal
input rate. You opt in by marking a block with cache_control: {
type: "ephemeral" } , which says “cache everything from the start of
the request up to and including this block.”
Three facts govern it:
It is a prefix match, and it is exact. The cache is keyed on the literal
sequence of tokens from the very beginning of the request. Change one
character anywhere in that prefix — one character — and everything
after the change is a cache miss. The order the API assembles things
in is tools , then system , then messages , so a tool schema you rebuild
with a different key order destroys the cache for everything behind it,
without saying so.

What It Knows and Forgets 69
There are two fixes, and they are the same fix at different scales.
Put the current truth in the context. If the request depends on
how something works today, include today’s documentation in the re-
quest rather than hoping. This is retrieval again, from the section above,
applied to knowledge rather than to code: fetch the small relevant part
and send it.
Pin what you can check. The model identifier in setup.ts is a
string the model has opinions about and no current knowledge of, and
so are your dependency versions. Keep anything a model might helpfully
“correct” for you in one place you own, where a change is deliberate.
Rule: Never let a model be the source of truth for a fact that has
a source of truth. Versions, identifiers, prices, schemas, flags: look
them up. The model is excellent at applying facts and unreliable at
storing them.

Pro Tip: Read verdict.md before git diff , always, in that or-
der. The verdict tells you what was supposed to happen; the diff
tells you what did. Read them the other way round and you are
reconstructing intent from code, which is what every job so far has
been arranged to avoid.
The judge is still a model
Everything Chapter 5 said applies here.
The judge hallucinates like anything else built on a model, and will
occasionally cite evidence that does not exist: a line number, a function

Talking to a Model 21
A prompt is the text you give the model to act on. In casual use people
mean the question they typed; in the API it is the whole input, meaning
every message in the array plus the field we are about to discuss.
The system prompt is a separate top-level system field carrying in-
structions about how to behave, as opposed to what to answer. It is not
a message and has no role; it sits outside the array. Two things make it
different from putting the same words in the first user message:
• It comes first, always, no matter how long the conversation grows.
• It reads as operator instruction rather than as something a partici-
pant in the conversation said, which makes it meaningfully harder
for later text to talk the model out of it.
In Chapter 7 you will build a reader whose job is to examine a change and
report problems, and its system prompt will say so.

model’s weights over an input to produce an output. It is the only
thing that happens when you call the API: no training, no learning, no

standard notation for describing the structure of JSON data — what
fields exist, what types they hold, which are required. What a tool’s

large language model — Chapter 1, 01-talking-to-a-model.md . A
very large mathematical function that takes a sequence of text and pro-

actly one question, asked in isolation, blind to the other lenses.

212 Appendix A: Glossary
request it makes. Nothing enforces it but you. The context window
protects the model; this protects you.
tool — Introduction, 00-introduction.md . A function in your program
that you have described to the model in a form it can request. The model
gains no capability it did not have — it gains a vocabulary for asking
you to do something.
tool schema — Chapter 2, 02-giving-the-model-hands.md . The
description of a tool: a name, a plain-English description, and an

Search the repository for messages.create and you will find nothing. It

Chapter 13
Inside a Plugin
This chapter builds a plugin, the smallest one that carries a piece of what
you wrote, and then reads quorum’s, directory by directory, as the same

Chapters 11 and 12 gave you the words: hook, skill, agent definition,

What the harness reads

knows.

From Yours to Shared 177
single change, and merging it turns the plan into history; nothing accu-

do. So the twentieth change is planned against the code, and against
whatever the person remembers, rather than against a maintained ac-
count of intended behaviour. Every criterion is local, every criterion is
per-change, and a contradiction between change three and change seven-

Nobody has measured how many defects the panel catches. The

The same is true of every rule in the last four

The next chapter moves the ones that can be mechanical into software

126 Running the Thing
It is slow. Ten process launches through npx tsx is a few seconds. This
lens will always be the slowest of the six.
It can be fooled by a program that fails without saying so. A
CLI that prints nothing and exits 0 looks calm in a transcript. This is
why the exit code line is recorded on every observation and why the
plan’s criteria should name the exit code as well as the output.
Six reports and no decision
You now have six files in work/fold-accents/reviews/ : five from read-
ing and one from running. Between them, perhaps fifteen findings, of
which perhaps ten are real, two are duplicates of each other in different
words, and three are wrong.
Nothing has been fixed, nothing has been decided, and no one has said
whether this change may proceed.

Chapter 9
Somebody Has to Decide
A judge decides what happens to each finding and records the reason, and
this chapter builds one. Six files hold perhaps fifteen findings between
them. Three of those are wrong, two are the same thing said twice, one
is a preference dressed as a defect, and somewhere in the pile are two
that genuinely must be fixed before this change goes anywhere.
The two ways of not deciding
There are exactly two ways to avoid making the decision.
Fix everything. Take all fifteen findings, hand them back, apply them
all. This fails for a reason that has nothing to do with effort: a third of
the findings are wrong, and applying a wrong finding actively damages
the change. You also lose the distinction between “must fix before this
ships” and “worth knowing about,” which means the next change carries
all fifteen again.
Ship it anyway.

The picture above is an agent : a program that calls a model in a loop,

A workflow is a fixed sequence of jobs that a piece of work passes

64 What It Knows and Forgets
Prompt caching stores the beginning of your request on Anthropic’s
servers so that identical beginnings on later requests do not have to be
processed again. Cached input is billed at a small fraction of the normal
input rate. You opt in by marking a block with cache_control: {
type: "ephemeral" } , which says “cache everything from the start of
the request up to and including this block.”
Three facts govern it:
It is a prefix match, and it is exact. The cache is keyed on the literal
sequence of tokens from the very beginning of the request. Change one
character anywhere in that prefix — one character — and everything
after the change is a cache miss. The order the API assembles things
in is tools , then system , then messages , so a tool schema you rebuild
with a different key order destroys the cache for everything behind it,
without saying so.

Stable content goes first. House rules, tool schemas, a large document
you are asking questions about: at the front, marked. Timestamps,
request IDs, the actual question: after the last marked block. If you put
new Date().toISOString() in your system prompt, your cache hit rate
is zero and nothing tells you.
You verify it with usage . cache_read_input_tokens is the only
proof you get. If it is zero across repeated requests that should share a
prefix, something is invalidating it, and the fastest way to find out what
is to shorten the prefix until the number goes up.
A prefix also has to be long enough to store. The floor is a few hundred
tokens and differs from model to model, and a request under it is not
cached and not warned about: written and cached both stay at zero.
The house rules alone are far under it, which is why budget.ts puts
loop.ts in the block.

The definition, before the code
An agent is a program that lets a model choose its own next action,
repeatedly, until the model decides it is finished.
The definition stops there: no autonomy, no planning, no reasoning, just
a loop with a model in the condition. Everything else people mean by
the word is a property of the tools you gave it and the instructions you
wrote.
The cycle that loop runs has a name of its own. The agentic loop is:
send the conversation, read the stop reason, execute any requested tools,
append the results, send again. One pass through that cycle is a turn .

Tokens
A token is the unit of text the model actually operates on: a chunk of
characters somewhere between a letter and a word. Common English
words are usually one token each, while rarer words are split into several,
and whitespace and punctuation usually ride along with a neighbouring
word. As a working rule of thumb for English prose, one token is about

Severity is a routing decision
Each finding carries one of three severities, and the point of having ex-
actly three is that each one names a different thing to do — not a different
degree of annoyance.
• blocker — this change must not proceed while this is true. Data
loss, a broken acceptance criterion, an unhandled case that reaches
users.
• major — real and worth fixing, though not necessarily in this
change, so it becomes recorded work instead.
• minor — worth someone knowing. Frequently a preference. Fre-
quently wrong.
Three is enough because the decision space is: stop, schedule, note.
